newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Bank Niaga nabs FRCD.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Bank Niaga nabs FRCD.

text.p: Asian debt markets ended a slow week slowly on Friday.
Indonesia's Bank Niaga set a US$40 million floating rate certificate of deposit issue. The issue has a final maturity of five years and puts and calls in years three and four.

The deal pays a margin of 80 basis points over the Singapore Interbank Offered Rate. Participating banks receive a fee of six basis points for underwriting and a management fee of 30 basis points on their final allotment.
Arrangers are Oversea Chinese Banking Corp and Sumitomo Finance Asia, which is the bookrunner.
South Korea's Asian Banking Corp is expected to launch its US$60 million FRCD issue later today in London.
The issue has a final maturity of five years with a put option in year three. Arrangers are KEB International London, Hanil Bank, WestLB and Bayerische Vereinsbank.
The issue is expected to have a coupon of LIBOR plus 55 basis points and an all-in return of 68-70 basis points.

Asian Banking Corp is the latest in a long line of Korean banks to take their tale to Europe. The top tier banks have had little trouble selling their story outside Asia, but merchant banks such as Asian Banking Corp are finding it more difficult, bankers said.
Allied Banking Corp of the Philippines has mandated Standard Chartered Investment Banking to arrange a US$50 million FRCD.
The three-year deal pays a coupon of 85 basis points over LIBOR and an all-in return of 92 basis points.
In other news from the Philippines, lead manager J.P. Morgan revealed that the country's new 20-year bond exchanged for Brady bonds attracted a geographically diverse group of investors.
Investors tendered US$678 million worth of collateralized bonds for the exchange programme. Of these, the Philippine government accepted US$635 million worth.
It also sold US$137 million new bonds to investors who did not have the old bonds to exchange but were willing to buy the bonds in cash, the Philippines announced Tuesday.
Of the investors that exchanged the bonds, 40 percent were from Asia, 35 percent from the U.S. and 25 percent from Europe, J.P. Morgan said.
Of those buying the bonds with new cash, 45 percent were from the U.S., 40 percent from Asia and 15 percent from Europe, the company said.
